guides.title: Africa and the Atlantic islands: linked voyages
guides.description: Ports, passages and return journeys linked to the same dated voyages already shown in the Americas and Pacific atlas.
guides.intro: Follow the voyages beyond the edge of one regional map. A departure port, an island stop and a return anchorage are parts of the same journey, with the same evidence and the same limits on what can be reconstructed.
guides.scope: This directory connects the existing voyage catalogue across regional guides. It does not add speculative stages or change the shared movie. Representative mapped anchors introduce the area; the complete dated regional list follows below.

map.scope: Selected documented geographic anchors across the whole regional connection area. Dates label particular visits, not the foundation of the ports. Offshore sightings retain their offshore status.

points.label: Porto Praia, Santiago
points.description: One documented anchor in HMS Beagle: selected ship itinerary, 1831–1836. Volume II, pp. 51–56. Regional port stay; small sounding movements are not represented. The complete connection list below retains other visits and their separate dates.

points.label: La Gomera, departure
points.description: One documented anchor in Columbus: selected first-voyage anchors, 1492–1493. Journal, 6 September 1492. Departure observation; the preceding island movements are not resolved. The complete connection list below retains other visits and their separate dates.

points.label: Funchal, Madeira
points.description: One documented anchor in Amundsen’s Fram · voyage to the Bay of Whales. Port call in the museum’s narrative chronology, where the crew learned about the change of plan. The complete connection list below retains other visits and their separate dates.

points.label: Cap-Vert peninsula anchorage
points.description: One documented anchor in Schouten and Le Maire · Eendracht around Cape Horn to Jacatra. Watering negotiations and stormy weather extended this coastal stay. The complete connection list below retains other visits and their separate dates.

points.label: Saint Helena anchorage
points.description: One documented anchor in Schouten · Amsterdam return from Java. Amsterdam’s date is retained separately from the other vessel’s earlier arrival. The 6 March Cape passage is only a guess in the source and has no plotted fix. The complete connection list below retains other visits and their separate dates.

points.label: Ascension Island roadstead
points.description: One documented anchor in Frank Wild’s Quest · Antarctic survey and Atlantic return. Wild anchored at Ascension to take coal. The complete connection list below retains other visits and their separate dates.

points.label: Cape Town
points.description: One documented anchor in Mawson’s Discovery · first BANZARE field season. Discovery set out on the first BANZARE voyage. The complete connection list below retains other visits and their separate dates.

points.label: Cape of Good Hope: Victoria offshore
points.description: One documented anchor in Magellan–Elcano expedition: selected anchors, 1519–1522. Somos Afro, Victoria return chronology. Offshore passage anchor; no port visit or precise track is implied. The complete connection list below retains other visits and their separate dates.

points.label: Port Louis, Mauritius
points.description: One documented anchor in HMS Beagle: selected ship itinerary, 1831–1836. Volume II, p. 638. The complete connection list below retains other visits and their separate dates.

points.label: Rodrigues departure
points.description: One documented anchor in Joshua Slocum · Spray circumnavigation. The dated departure is used; the approximate length of stay is not turned into a falsely exact arrival. The complete connection list below retains other visits and their separate dates.

paragraphs.text: The dated lists retain each itinerary’s original descriptions. A documented landfall, a roadstead stay and a passage offshore are different kinds of evidence. Where the source leaves a gap, a linking animation is an illustration rather than a recovered daily ship track.

The same port can occur more than once in a journey, and several expeditions can share a harbor. Keeping those visits separate makes it possible to follow preparation, outbound movement and return without turning a port into one timeless event.
